4.6. pass Statements ¶

The pass statement does nothing. It can be used when a statement is
required syntactically but the program requires no action. For example:

>>> while True:

top.text:
4.6. pass Statements ¶

The pass statement does nothing. It can be used when a statement is
required syntactically but the program requires no action. For example:

>>> while True:
...     pass  # Busy-wait for keyboard interrupt (Ctrl+C)
...

This is commonly used for creating minimal classes:

>>>

top.section: 4. More Control Flow Tools ¶ > 4.6. pass Statements ¶
top.text:
For this last case, many people use the ellipsis literal ... instead of
pass. This use has no special meaning to Python, and is not part of
the language definition (you could use any constant expression here), but
... is used conventionally as a placeholder body as well.
See The Ellipsis Object.

top.section: 7. Input and Output ¶ > 7.1. Fancier Output Formatting ¶ > 7.1.1. Formatted String Literals ¶
top.text:
7.1.1. Formatted String Literals ¶

Formatted string literals (also called f-strings for
short) let you include the value of Python expressions inside a string by
prefixing the string with f or F and writing expressions as
{expression}.

top.section: 7. Input and Output ¶ > 7.1. Fancier Output Formatting ¶
top.text:
There are several ways to format output.

To use formatted string literals, begin a string
with f or F before the opening quotation mark or triple quotation mark.
Inside this string, you can write a Python expression between { and }
characters that can refer to variables or literal values.

top.section: 7. Input and Output ¶ > 7.1. Fancier Output Formatting ¶ > 7.1.2. The String format() Method ¶
